useCases.n: AI design critique of UI screens
useCases.d: Instead of checking fixed rules, the AI writes open-ended design feedback on a UI screenshot, the way a senior designer might in a critique session, pointing to specific regions and giving quality ratings. useCases.d: AI 'personas' are generated in bulk and each one is turned into an agent that tries to complete tasks on a designed website or prototype, producing data that resembles a usability test. In UXAgent, a persona generator feeds an LLM agent that operates a real Chrome browser; outputs include action traces, reasoning traces, video recordings and an interface for 'interviewing' the agent about its choices. useCases.d: AI predicts where people's eyes will go on a design, producing a colored 'heatmap' without recruiting anyone for an eye-tracking study. useCases.ds: When the product being designed is itself an AI feature (a chatbot, voice assistant or on-screen helper), designers build prototypes that call a real language model so test participants experience actual AI behavior rather than scripted screens.
useCases.dr: In the CMU approach, designers replay recorded user-session videos to an LLM, refine its instructions, rate candidate responses, and in live 'hybrid Wizard-of-Oz' sessions a human approves AI responses before they reach the participant. The output is a tested prompt strategy and a prototype whose AI behavior has been checked in context. It sits at the boundary of making and testing, because the AI's responses are part of the artifact being evaluated. NN/g (2026) similarly notes that AI prototyping makes it feasible to include AI-generated responses in prototypes and test them with users before deployment, while cautioning that this shows what became feasible, not that the research is better.

useCases.d: Instead of describing a screen in words, the designer gives the AI a picture or file: a photo of a hand sketch, a mockup screenshot, or a link to a Figma frame. It sits where design meets build: turning an existing sketch or mockup into something clickable, or into code a developer can start from.
